title: WOULD JESUS RECOGNIZE THE CHRISTIANITY WE PRACTICE TODAY?
paragraphs: WOULD JESUS RECOGNIZE THE CHRISTIANITY WE PRACTICE TODAY?
We learned how to look Christian. Jesus is still asking whether we actually know Him.
There is a question most Christians would rather answer about somebody else.
Not because it is complicated.
Because it gets dangerously close to the heart.

If Jesus Christ walked visibly into our churches today—past the LED screens, worship sets, carefully designed stages, Christian merchandise, livestream cameras, conferences, podcasts, bestselling books, theological arguments, viral reels, political debates, ministry brands, and perfectly curated Christian profiles—would He recognize what we are doing as the life He actually called us to live?
Before you answer too quickly, remember something uncomfortable.
Some of the people most certain that they represented God were the very people who failed to recognize God when He stood in front of them.
They knew Scripture.
They prayed.
They fasted.
They gave.
They defended doctrine.
They possessed religious influence.
They could recognize violations of tradition from across a room.
And yet Jesus looked directly at religious people who appeared clean and said:
“Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!”
The Greek word translated “hypocrites” is ὑποκριταί (hypokritai), from ὑποκριτής (hypokritēs), a word associated with an actor or one playing a role.
That should make every Christian uncomfortable before it makes us judgmental.
Because this article is not primarily about “those fake Christians.”
It is about me.
It is about you.
It is about the terrifying possibility of becoming skilled at performing Christianity while slowly becoming unfamiliar with Christ.
And perhaps the question is not merely:
Would Jesus recognize Christianity today?
Perhaps the more frightening question is:
Would Jesus recognize Himself in me?
Sit with that.
Because you can wear a cross without carrying one.
You can post Bible verses while refusing to forgive somebody.
You can lift your hands during worship while keeping your heart closed to the person who wounded you.
You can defend biblical marriage while destroying your own home with pride.
You can condemn sexual sin while secretly feeding lust through a glowing screen.
You can speak passionately about holiness while gossiping about another believer the moment they leave the room.
You can know worship songs and barely know prayer.
You can know Christian vocabulary and barely know Christ.
You can say “God bless you” while secretly hoping someone fails.
You can expose everybody else's darkness while negotiating with your own.
And yes...
you can build a Christian audience while quietly losing your first love.
That is why Jesus' words in Matthew 7 are among the most sobering sentences ever spoken:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven.”
Then comes the sentence that should destroy casual Christianity:
“I never knew you.”
The Greek is:

οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
oudepote egnōn hymas
“I never knew you.”
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say, “You never looked religious enough.”
The people standing before Him appeal to religious activity.
They call Him “Lord.”
They point to things they did in His name.
Yet their résumé cannot substitute for relationship and obedience.
Christianity was never supposed to be a costume worn around an unchanged heart.
Jesus did not die so sinners could learn Christian vocabulary while remaining comfortably enslaved to the sins from which He came to save them.
The angel's announcement concerning Christ in Matthew 1:21 was astonishingly direct:
“He shall save his people from their sins.”
Not merely from embarrassment.
Not merely from consequences.
Not merely from hell while leaving sin enthroned over their present lives.
From their sins.
Grace is not God's permission to remain chained.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward people who could never rescue themselves—and in Christ, that grace begins making redeemed people new.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith...”
And then only a few words later:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works.”
Grace saves.
And saving grace does not leave the redeemed exactly where it found them.
This matters because modern Christianity can sometimes reduce the Gospel to something painfully small:
Believe enough to feel safe.
Attend enough to feel faithful.
Give enough to feel generous.
Post enough Scripture to appear spiritual.
Avoid the sins your Christian circle considers especially disgraceful.
Then continue arranging the rest of your life largely around yourself.
But listen to Jesus.
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.”
The Greek expression behind “deny himself” is:

ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτόν
aparnēsasthō heauton
It carries the force of denying or disowning oneself.
Jesus was not advertising self-improvement.
He was calling people to surrender.
That does not mean Christians earn salvation through suffering, discipline, charitable works, or religious performance. Scripture crushes that idea.
We are saved by grace through faith, “not of works, lest any man should boast.”
The cross of Christ is sufficient.
His blood is sufficient.
His righteousness—not ours—is the foundation of our acceptance before God.
But the Christ who saves us also calls us to follow Him.
We cannot purchase grace with obedience.
But when grace captures a human heart, obedience begins to matter because Christ matters.
Jesus said:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.”
That is where this becomes personal.
Because perhaps Christianity's greatest scandal is not that sinners still enter churches.
Thank God they do.
The Church should be full of people with histories.
Addicts.
Adulterers.
Liars.
Pornography survivors.
Former unbelievers.
Broken marriages.
Proud people.
Greedy people.
Traumatized people.
People carrying shame they cannot explain.
People who destroyed years of their lives.
People who failed after promising God they never would again.
People who walked away and somehow found themselves standing at the church door again.
That is not the scandal.
That is exactly where grace belongs.
The scandal begins when we make peace with the chains Jesus died to break.
When repentance becomes embarrassing.
When holiness becomes “legalism” merely because it confronts something we do not want to surrender.
When grace becomes an excuse instead of a miracle.
When Christianity becomes more concerned with looking respectable than becoming Christlike.
The New Testament word commonly translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), from μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It speaks of repentance—a profound turning of mind and direction toward God.
Jesus began His public proclamation with a call to repentance:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
Repentance and Gospel were never enemies.
Repentance is not God standing over broken people screaming, “Make yourself worthy.”
It is God calling sinners to stop running toward death and come home through Christ.
And this is where some people misunderstand Jesus.
They remember Him eating with sinners.
They forget why sinners were drawn to Him.
He did not demand that wounded people repair themselves before approaching Him.
He touched lepers.
He received the despised.
He welcomed children.
He spoke with the socially rejected.
He ate with tax collectors and sinners.
He showed extraordinary compassion toward people religious society had reduced to labels.
But His compassion was never indifference toward sin.
To the woman caught in adultery, He gave mercy—and then said:
“Go, and sin no more.”
Grace did not throw the stone.
Grace also did not call the bondage freedom.
That is Jesus.
Full of grace.
Full of truth.
Not fifty percent mercy and fifty percent holiness.
He is perfectly both.
And perhaps we have spent years trying to choose the half of Jesus that makes us most comfortable.
Some churches want a Jesus who comforts but never confronts.
Others preach a Jesus who seems to confront but rarely sounds compassionate.
Some believers speak endlessly about truth without love.
Others speak endlessly about love while becoming frightened of truth.
But John did not say Jesus was full of whichever quality matched our personality.
“The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us... full of grace and truth.”

χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας
charitos kai alētheias
Grace and truth.
Together.
Always.
So would Jesus recognize Christianity today?
There is no honest way to answer that with one sweeping judgment about every church and every believer.
Christ has faithful people across nations, denominations, cultures, languages, congregations, homes, prisons, hospitals, villages, cities, and places the internet will never notice.
There are pastors faithfully preaching Scripture without fame.
There are mothers praying over sleeping children when nobody is watching.
There are fathers quietly choosing integrity.
There are young believers deleting what feeds temptation.
There are Christians forgiving wounds that would make most people understand their bitterness.
There are missionaries serving where nobody applauds.
There are elderly saints whose knees have grown weak but whose prayers remain fierce.
There are believers feeding hungry people without photographing the meal.
There are Christians resisting temptation tonight while nobody knows how difficult the battle has become.
There are former addicts whispering the name of Jesus because they know exactly what another relapse could cost.
There are wounded believers returning to church even though church people once wounded them.
There are disciples nobody follows online whom heaven knows intimately.
Jesus knows His sheep.
The problem is not that authentic Christianity disappeared.
The question is whether we personally are practicing it.
Because Jesus repeatedly moved attention away from appearances and toward the heart.
Human beings are impressed by visibility.
God sees secrecy.
We count followers.
God examines faithfulness.
We notice platforms.
God notices motives.
We celebrate charisma.
God values character.
We photograph generosity.
Jesus spoke about giving where the left hand does not know what the right hand is doing.
We announce spiritual victories.
Jesus told stories about humility.
We build personal brands.
John the Baptist said:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
Read that again.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
That sentence is almost violently opposed to the instincts of an age built around self-promotion.
Even Christian self-promotion.
More followers.
More recognition.
More influence.
More visibility.
More applause.
More me.
Yet the Gospel keeps whispering:
More Christ.
Less me.
And there is another uncomfortable test.
Jesus said the world would recognize His disciples by something surprisingly ordinary:
“By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.”
Not by how viciously they destroy strangers in comment sections.
Not by how expertly they humiliate another believer.
Not by how many Bible verses they can weaponize.
Not by how quickly they pronounce judgment on someone whose story they barely understand.
Love.
But biblical love is not cowardice.
Love can confront.
Love can warn.
Love can establish boundaries.
Love can refuse deception.
Love can call sin what God calls sin.
But biblical love does not secretly enjoy crushing the sinner.
There is a difference between grieving over somebody's sin and enjoying somebody's humiliation.
Jesus wept over Jerusalem.
Some Christians would rather win the argument.
And maybe that is the moment this article stops being comfortable.
Because somebody hurt you.
Maybe badly.
And you have been calling your bitterness “discernment.”
Someone embarrassed you.
Betrayed you.
Abandoned you.
Lied about you.
Cheated on you.
Used you.
Perhaps somebody from church did it.
And somewhere along the way, you discovered that resentment can disguise itself as righteousness.
You pray.
You worship.
You read Scripture.
But their name still changes your heartbeat.
You imagine the day they finally get what they deserve.
Then Jesus says:
“Love your enemies.”
And suddenly Christianity is no longer inspirational.
It is cruciform.
This is where the cross stops being jewelry.
Because the cross means Jesus Christ loved His enemies while His enemies were killing Him.
“Father, forgive them...”
That does not mean abuse should be tolerated.
It does not mean reconciliation is always immediately possible or safe.
Forgiveness and restored trust are not identical.
Wisdom and boundaries matter.
But hatred cannot be our permanent home.
The Gospel will eventually knock on that locked room too.
And perhaps there is another room.
The one nobody knows about.
The browser history.
The secret conversation.
The bottle.
The fantasy.
The jealousy.
The money.
The pride.
The private compromise.
The hidden relationship.
The habit you promised God was over.
The wound you keep medicating with something that is slowly becoming your master.
You have learned how to hide it.
People still think you are strong.
You still know exactly what to say when someone asks how you are doing.
“Blessed.”
But God knows.
And strangely, that is not merely terrifying.
It is beautiful.
Because the One who knows the worst thing about you is the One who went to the cross for sinners.
Romans does not say Christ died for us once we became impressive.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While.
We.
Were.
Yet.
Sinners.
This is the heartbeat of Christianity.
Not good people climbing toward God.
God coming down to rescue people who could not save themselves.
The eternal Son took flesh.
Jesus lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose bodily from the dead.
And because He lives, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
He had promised loyalty.
Then fear exposed him.
“I know not the man.”
Those words must have echoed through his mind after the rooster crowed.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, Christ met the disciple who had failed Him.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Not to call betrayal harmless.
Jesus brought Peter back to the place of love and calling.
“Lovest thou me?”
Then:
“Feed my sheep.”
Failure was not given the final sentence.
Jesus was.
That is the Gospel.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting evil as good.
Not by rewriting sin as harmless.
Not by rewriting rebellion as authenticity.
Jesus rewrites everything by redeeming sinners.
He turns persecutors into apostles.
The ashamed into witnesses.
The enslaved into people learning freedom.
The proud into servants.
The wounded into healers.
The spiritually dead into people made alive in Christ.
Maybe you clicked this article expecting an indictment of modern Christianity.
Perhaps you expected names.
Denominations.
Pastors.
Scandals.
Culture wars.
Hypocrites.
But the Holy Spirit may be asking something far more dangerous than:
“What is wrong with Christianity?”
He may be asking:
“What have you refused to surrender to Christ?”
What have you refused to surrender?
Your anger?
Your sexuality?
Your pride?
Your secret addiction?
Your reputation?
Your money?
Your relationship?
Your need to be admired?
Your unforgiveness?
Your theology of convenience?
Your obsession with being right?
Your fear of people?
Your hunger for attention?
Your comfortable Christianity?
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending.
Good.
Not because exhaustion is holy, but because pretending is a terrible place to live.
You do not need to impress Jesus.
You need Jesus.
You do not need a better Christian costume.
You need a surrendered heart.
You do not need another inspirational quote to survive until Sunday.
You need the living Christ.
Come to Him.
Confess honestly.
Repent genuinely.
Trust Him completely.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
And then get up and follow Him.
One surrendered decision at a time.
One forgiven enemy at a time.
One deleted temptation at a time.
One honest prayer at a time.
One act of obedience nobody applauds at a time.
One morning when you choose Scripture instead of the thing that has been discipling your desires.
One night when you whisper, “Jesus, help me,” instead of returning willingly to your chains.
Christianity does not become authentic when Christians become flawless.
If perfection before coming to Christ were required, none of us could come.
Authentic Christianity begins with Christ Himself.
And discipleship means we keep returning to Him—repenting when we fall, receiving grace, learning obedience, loving His Word, loving people, carrying our crosses, and being transformed by His Spirit.
So perhaps the question we should carry from this moment is no longer simply:
“Would Jesus recognize the Christianity we practice today?”
Make it painfully personal.
“Jesus... do You recognize Your life being formed in mine?”
Not my profile.
Not my denomination.
Not my Christian vocabulary.
Not the verse in my bio.
Not the cross around my neck.
Not the sermons I share.
Not what everyone thinks about me.
My actual life.
My secret life.
My thoughts.
My relationships.
My forgiveness.
My money.
My purity.
My treatment of people who cannot benefit me.
My response when nobody is watching.
My obedience when obedience costs something.
My heart.
And if that question exposed something hidden, do not hide again.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your wound.
God already knows the story.
Sometimes the first courageous step is simply admitting that you need someone to stand with you before Him.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this, send this article to them.
Not as an accusation.
As an invitation.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Because some truths need to find us again after the emotion has faded.
Not to purchase God's favor.
Not because supporting a ministry earns blessing, salvation, forgiveness, or standing before God.
Jesus purchased salvation. We cannot.
Supporting Gospel work is not a substitute for worship.
It can be one practical expression of stewardship when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for Christ rather than human recognition.
If that deeper journey is where you know you need to go, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has drifted.
Invite the believer quietly struggling.
Invite the person angry at God.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the skeptic.
Even invite the person who does not believe yet.
Because Christianity does not need another generation merely skilled at appearing Christian.
We need men and women who have encountered Jesus Christ so deeply that grace changes how they live when nobody is watching.
And tonight, before you judge what Christianity has become in everybody else...
ask Jesus what Christianity has become in you.

Because when all the stages go dark, the Christian profiles disappear, the arguments end, the applause stops, and every carefully constructed religious image finally falls away, only one thing will matter:
Whether beneath everything we called Christianity, we were actually following Christ.
